item.title: Raising the cost of attacking journalists
item.description:
2. november 2026

Kjersti Løken Stavrum, CEO of the Tinius Trust, gave opening remarks at the 12th International Conference on the Safety of Journalists at OsloMet. Read her speech here:

Good morning. Thank you to MEKK at OsloMet, the Fritt Ord Foundation and UNESCO Norway for the invitation. And for bringing all of us together on this International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against journalists.

The vest marked PRESS was meant to carry a simple message: this person is a civilian, here to observe and report, not to fight.

In too many places today, that message is no longer respected. For some, the vest itself has become a reason to shoot.

Many in this room know the figures from the Committee to Protect Journalists better than I do, so let me pick out only a few of the numbers. Since October 2023, CPJ has documented at least 247 journalists and media workers killed in Gaza, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran. To put that in a Norwegian perspective: the Norwegian Union of Journalists has around 8,600 members. A loss on that scale here would mean roughly one in every 35 of them – in three years.

In Gaza, where international reporters are still barred from entering independently, local journalists have carried the burden of reporting the war to the world - and many have paid with their lives. Journalists have also been killed in Sudan and in Ukraine, increasingly by drones. So far this year, CPJ has registered 34 journalists and media workers killed in cases confirmed or suspected to be connected to their work.

Behind each number is a person who stayed when others left – or had to leave. And each killing is more than a personal tragedy. It is an attack on the public's right to know. A war without independent witnesses is a war in which anything can be claimed, and nothing can be checked.

Two questions therefore need answering at the same time. How can the risk be raised for those who put journalists in danger? And what can the profession itself do to strengthen its own safety? The law is, thankfully, on the side of journalists.

What is missing is a wider recognition that attacking a journalist is not only a legal violation, but a moral one - a breach of everyone's right to know what is happening in the world.

I see four things that can make a difference. The first concerns those who commit the attacks; the other three concern the profession itself.

First: those who commit crimes against journalists must be pursued far more systematically. Journalists in war are civilians, and deliberately attacking them is a war crime. Yet of the journalists CPJ found to have been deliberately killed for their work last year, no one has been held accountable in a single case. That must change. It requires careful documentation from the very first hour, states willing to investigate and prosecute, and the patience to pursue cases over many years - because the perpetrators count on the world forgetting. Impunity is not merely an absence of consequences. It is an invitation. I think there is a need for civil society to restructure the way we approach those crimes.

Second: the recognition of the professional journalist must be strengthened. It is less clear today who is reporting in the field. That anyone with a phone can document what is happening is, in principle, a strength. Much of what the world knows from conflict zones comes from people who never trained as reporters. But it must not mean that more people are exposed to danger without training, protection or an editorial organization behind them.

Nor must it blur the line between those who report and those who fight. This year, CPJ reviewed its records from Gaza and removed several names after establishing that they had taken part in combat. That matters, because every misuse of press credentials weakens the protection of everyone who depends on them.

"Journalist" is not a protected title. That is precisely why professional journalists must guard their integrity and professionalism to the utmost. In conflict, the credibility of the profession is part of its protection.

Third: professional journalists must hold themselves to professional ethics. In practice, that means verifying before publishing - even under intense pressure to be first, and even when the material comes from a side one sympathizes with. It means – as you well know - separating facts from opinions, and what is known from what is believed. It means independence from the parties in the conflict: not wearing their uniform, not carrying their weapons, not taking their instructions or their money. It means protecting sources, who in war may risk their lives by speaking. It means respecting the dignity of victims and of the dead. And it means correcting errors openly and quickly.

Better still is to belong to an established and recognized system of press ethics – a shared code, and a press council or similar body where anyone can complain and where decisions are made public. That turns a personal commitment into one that others can hold to account, and it gives the claim to be a professional journalist real substance.

These are not bureaucratic rules. In war, they are what separates journalism from propaganda - and the protection the law offers rests on that distinction.

Fourth: professional journalists must be as open and transparent as possible about their work and their findings. That means explaining how they know what they know, saying what they could not verify, and showing their sources where it is safe to do so. It means explaining the choices behind the account they present, so that audiences can understand it - and challenge it.

Journalism must not be hidden political activism. Bias must be fought, including one's own. And fighting bias means more than balance in a single story. It means understanding the depth and complexity of a war: its history, its many parties, the civilians caught between them. This matters most in the conflicts that last for years, where audiences grow exhausted and lose interest, and where coverage easily shrinks to a few familiar images and a simple story of right and wrong.

Staying with a conflict and continuing to explain it when attention has moved elsewhere, is part of the professional obligation.

Transparency is not a weakness. At a time when every image is contested and every report is dismissed as fake by someone, it is how trust is earned.

This is a critical time for professional journalism. Information itself has become a battlefield, and those who wage war also fight over the narrative. Journalists who insist on facts stand in their way.

Professional journalists do not feed hatred and polarization. Their task is to inform and enlighten, and to give people who disagree a shared foundation of facts - for the good of democracy and a future peace. That is why they are targeted. And that is why protecting them, and making those who attack them pay a price, is a task for all of us.

I wish you all a fruitful conference – and every journalist reporting from a war zone today a safe return.

item.title: The Tinius Trust joins international effort on traceable information in the age of AI
item.description:
29. september 2026

The Tinius Trust is joining the venture studio Signals at Scale as a partner. The studio defines the problems to be solved in the emerging AI-mediated information ecosystem and funds those building systems that make the information reaching users through artificial intelligence possible to verify.

Signals at Scale was founded by Shuwei Fang, a Shorenstein Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School, and David Caswell, formerly head of AI innovation at BBC News Labs. Signals at Scale identifies challenges in the emerging ecosystem, assembles small teams around each challenge, funds them and sets deadlines.

The studio starts from the assumption of a greatly expanded information ecosystem, with vastly more information flowing through it. Functions such as traceability, verification and compensation look very different if information output is 100 or 1,000 times what manual workflows produce today, or if consumption becomes dramatically more personalised and relevant.

Why the Tinius Trust is taking part

As a long-term media owner, the Tinius Trust wants to help build this infrastructure for crediting and paying sources.

"The Tinius Trust works to secure good conditions for free media, as our articles of association require. For a long time that has meant legislation and source protection. Now a large part of the framework is set in the technology itself, in how language models choose sources, what they credit and how errors are corrected. No common standard is in place yet, and nobody knows where it will be made. Signals at Scale is one of several attempts. We would rather take part in those attempts than wait for an answer from the technology giants," says Nicklas Stavnar, Head of Foresight at the Tinius Trust.

What the partnership involves

The partnership runs for two years, from 1 September 2026. The Tinius Trust contributes around NOK 3.1 million a year.

Earlier work with the same researchers

This is the second time the Tinius Trust has worked with Caswell and Fang. In 2025 the trust funded and took part in the project AI in Journalism Futures 2025. The project is published here

item.title: Adele Matheson Mestad joins the board of the Tinius Trust
item.description:
28. mai 2026

Adele Matheson Mestad. former Director of the Norwegian National Human Rights Institution, now partner at BAHR, is a new member of the Board at the Tinius Trust. "With Adele Matheson Mestad, we gain solid knowledge of human rights, freedom of expression and technological development, and above all, a wise mind with fresh perspectives," says Board Chair Ole Jacob Sunde.

Mestad replaces Gunilla Asker, a business leader and professional board member with extensive experience from the media, retail and tech sectors. 

"I want to extend a great thanks to Gunilla Asker for the force she has been on the board. She has continually reminded us to see the media through the eyes of the reader and the user. That still holds true," says Ole Jacob Sunde.

item.title: Raoul Grünthal new Chair of the Tinius Trust
item.description:
28. mai 2026

Raoul Grünthal has been elected as the new Chair of the Tinius Trust, effective 17 June. "I really look forward to leading this board in an incredibly exciting time," he says.

The board of the Tinius Trust has appointed Raoul Grünthal as new Chair, succeeding Ole Jacob Sunde, who steps down due to the age limit at the annual board meeting on 17 June 2026. Raoul Grünthal is a long-standing media executive with a background from Schibsted, among others. He is currently Chair of the Danish JP/Politiken Media Group, until the Annual General Meeting in the spring of 2027.

"Well-managed media ownership is more important now than ever before. That gives me strong motivation to take on this important role, and to work for the important purpose the Tinius Trust represents. Free and independent journalism, freedom of expression and democracy are values that must be held high and defended in our time”, says Raoul Grünthal.

"We have had good discussions in the board, and we are fully confident that Raoul is the right person to take over as Chair," says outgoing Chair Ole Jacob Sunde.

"I know Raoul from my time as Chair of Schibsted. He has respect and understanding for the editorial teams' work and sound judgement in strategic decisions. He led Schibsted's transition to digital platforms and understands that our media are in the midst of a new technological challenge that requires long-term thinking. That aligns well with the Trust's purpose of securing free and independent journalism while ensuring financial sustainability," he continues.

More about Raoul Grünthal

item.title: Court gives green light to Norwegian state mass surveillance
item.description:
26. mars 2025

Today, the Oslo District Court fully supported the Norwegian state in the case regarding the Norwegian Intelligence Service's mass surveillance, brought by the Tinius Trust and editor Tom Erik Thorsen.

– We took this case to court because it addresses a fundamental question: How far can the state go in monitoring our digital communication? With this ruling, we believe the state has been granted excessively broad powers, says Kjersti Løken Stavrum, CEO of the Tinius Trust.

The decision will be thoroughly reviewed, and an appeal will be considered.

– In the times we live in, it is particularly important to stand up for liberal values. This is a matter of principle with significant societal implications. We will, therefore, carefully evaluate our next steps, Stavrum adds.

– Our clients are naturally disappointed, but we must now carefully review the 67-page judgment together with them. Only then can we form a clear opinion on the detailed reasoning of the court, says lawyer Jon Wessel-Aas, who represents the Tinius Trust.

Download the judgment (PDF in Norwegian).

---

Contact Tinius Trust: Head of Communications, Marius Bakke, mb@tinius.com, +47 40235097

Contact Glittertind Law Firm (legal representative): Lawyer Jon Wessel-Aas, jwa@glittertind.no, +47 97062120

---

Download images from the court proceedings here: https://www.flickr.com/photos/tiniustrust/albums/72177720322297396/
Images from the trial may be freely used when reporting on the case with credit to photographer Petter Berntsen/NTB Kommunikasjon.

Read all about the lawsuit on tinius.com: https://www.tinius.com/no/soksmalet-mot-staten
